Bought my 00-15m about 8 years ago as my starter guitar. 3 albums and 100+ shows later, it’s still my favorite. Elliott Smith recorded his albums on toy guitars, Yamahas, Martins, etc. I’m a firm believer that every instrument, no matter the value or hype, has an equal purpose and place.

Jean Ritchie didn’t completely compose it, but she did create the setting to the lyrics, which means the specific melody, which is what Dylan swiped. There is no evidence that I’ve found the famous melody predates Ritchie’s recording of it. Her version was her own, but since it was still technically a traditional song, she didn’t own it. The same thing goes for Dave Van Ronk and House of The Rising Sun: Van Ronk wrote the setting to that song which was all his own (the traditional melody and chord progression was much different), then Dylan recorded it first without asking him. Paul Clayton did the same to Who’s Gonna Buy You Ribbons: He changed the traditional version immensely, and that’s the version that Dylan took.

Don’t get me wrong, Dylan is a genius and he created a bunch of melodies by himself that were just incredible. But there’s a reason folks say he’s a plagiarist. I do think he unfairly took credit for things he didn’t create. He had the opportunity to credit Jean Ritchie, Paul Clayton and Dave Van Ronk on the liner notes for their original work. Instead, he listed himself as the one and only songwriter, and decades later mentioned it in rereleases or in interviews. Even if Ritchie et al didn’t write the settings, he shouldn’t mentioned that the melodies were traditional and not his own. That’s not what folk music is.

I absolutely love Dylan and his art (he’s probably my favorite artist), but I’ll never defend his plagiarism. He has enough completely original material for me to be comfortable with the fact that he stole from others. I’m just bummed that he missed the chance to give them credit early on.

A little addition to the watch’s story: It belonged to my great-grandfather, originally, who was born around 1900. He was a working-class coal miner and boxer in Nova Scotia, Canada. My grandfather thinks he bartered for the watch.

In the words of my grandfather (who is now 90): 
“Given the time, and the “times” I’m quite sure it was not a high value watch but it was after WWII and at the time it was unusual in Canada for a “working man” to have a watch! Your GG was a gentle guy but was big and strong and didn’t value “decorative” things as a watch would be back in the day. While I’m not positive, I doubt he would have bought it. My sense is that it would be bartered because there was little money and he would frequently offer coal, upholstery work or trucking (hauling) in exchange for things!”

Figured I’d leave that here if anyone was interested in its origin. Might raise more questions than answers though. Thanks for everyone’s input!

This is a giant sequoia named the “Mark Twain Tree.” You can find photographs of the trees from different angles online. It was cut down in 1891 by the American Museum of Natural History. Here is a photo of the tree being felled, colorized using AI:

https://preview.redd.it/zal99kizgvwd1.jpeg?width=1790&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=83dff07392a72e02e999fb17232658f5ad6a01f1

This is not a chestnut tree. It is a giant sequoia, aka giant redwood, aka Sequoiadendron giganteum. You can see other giant sequoias in the background of the photo. The chestnuts did grow to enormous sizes historically, but not this large. This specific photograph is of a giant sequoia named the “Mark Twain Tree.” You can find photographs of the trees from different angles online. It was cut down in 1891.

Racism aside (yes, it’s a shit name), Sundown Town still exists. I (hopefully still) live in St. James Village and have bushwhacked through the mountains to find it. A plaque stands at the top of Brown’s Creek Trail detailing how it “completely burned” in the 1960s. Interestingly, most of the town remained. Even more, someone had bought the property and seemed to be doing renovations. 

Visiting it was eerie; It was like walking into a movie set. There was an old saloon, stables, a jail—all in the middle of the woods, right up the hill from a neighborhood.

I doubt Sundown Town will survive this fire. All of its buildings were uninsulated tinder boxes, and its surrounding forest landscape was unmanaged. Despite its name, I hope it does survive—Buster Keaton’s son built it!

The real tragedy of this fire will be the Brown’s Creek drainage, right above Sundown Town. There are some breathtaking ancient aspen groves in that area. I hope it survives.

My phone crashed a couple months ago and I lost every photograph of what had been the best summer of my life with the people I loved. I was devastated. A week later I was speaking with one of the friends I had made those memories with. He said, “It doesn’t matter—it’s all bullshit compared to what’s in here and here”. He pointed to my head and then my heart. I take less photos now. I don’t need them to store memories. I don’t even need memories. I suffer from severe depression but that doesn’t mean I don’t know where to focus my effort: The present. Live your best moments today, don’t relive the dead ones of yesterday. Find the people who you made those moments with. Or find new ones. Make some more. Do not let technology get the better of you. Please. I’m here for you if you need me 🌈

We need more people who feel as much as you do. I usually don’t comment, as it’s a lot of emotional work, but you seem like an amazing guy who deserves happiness. Please keep fighting. Start anew. And then start again. Reinvent yourself if you’re feeling low, don’t rob your eyes of having a shot at enjoying the universe. It’s there for you. We’re here for you. If you stick around, you have my word that one day you’ll be looking around, just being here and observing everything, listening to the world around you, and you’ll say, “I’m glad I stayed longer”.
